messages.subject: "SE=T" in MIRT
parts:
Hi, Phil

I am trying to do this model;

dif_gaikou<-'
f1=1-14
f2=4,12,13,14
'
result_gaikou_dif<-multipleGroup(data_gaikou,dif_gaikou,group=group,method="MHRM",SE=T);result_gaikou_dif
coef(result_gaikou_dif)

So, this result is ;

---
Full-information item factor analysis with 2 factor(s).
Converged within 0.001 tolerance after 469 MHRM iterations.
mirt version: 1.18 
M-step optimizer: NR 

Information matrix estimated with method: MHRM
Condition number of information matrix = 2946.158
Second-order test: model is not a maximum, or the information matrix is too inaccurate

Log-likelihood = -14340.75, SE = 0.413
AIC = 29161.5; AICc = 29276.84
BIC = 30391.76; SABIC = 29629.42
> coef(result_gaikou_dif)
$D1
$D1$f1001
           a1 a2    d1     d2     d3
par     3.352  0 5.210  0.140 -6.008
CI_2.5    NaN NA 4.505 -0.304 -6.300
CI_97.5   NaN NA 5.916  0.583 -5.716

$D1$f1002
           a1 a2    d1    d2     d3
par     2.521  0 4.732 -0.35 -4.485
CI_2.5  2.098 NA 4.433 -0.77 -5.352
CI_97.5 2.944 NA 5.030  0.07 -3.619

----

"Second-order test: model is not a maximum, or the information matrix is too inaccurate" is error?

thanks,

Yutaro

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: "SE=T" in MIRT
parts:
This can happen with the MHRM, particularly if the parameter estimates are more extreme (e.g, your slope of 3.352 is pretty large by most IRT standards....it's basically a step function). You can try lowering the SEtol input to the technical list, or switch to the 'FMHRM' SE.type to use a fixed number of Monte Carlo samples for the information matrix. HTH.

Phil

2016年10月11日火曜日 23時28分47秒 UTC+9 Phil Chalmers:

This can happen with the MHRM, particularly if the parameter estimates are more extreme (e.g, your slope of 3.352 is pretty large by most IRT standards....it's basically a step function). You can try lowering the SEtol input to the technical list, or switch to the 'FMHRM' SE.type to use a fixed number of Monte Carlo samples for the information matrix. HTH.
Phil

Hi Yutaro,

The fact that it took more than 500 EM cycles (and in your case, 5000!) to converge generally indicates that there is very little empirical information for the specified model. So, it likely means that the model that you have defined is not a good fit to the data. My guess is that the second f2 factor is not well defined. How does the model work when only the single factor is used? And how well does it fit (e.g., via functions like M2() )? 

Phil

This can happen with the MHRM, particularly if the parameter estimates are more extreme (e.g, your slope of 3.352 is pretty large by most IRT standards....it's basically a step function). Phil

2016年10月12日水曜日 13時39分03秒 UTC+9 Phil Chalmers:

Hi Yutaro,

The fact that it took more than 500 EM cycles (and in your case, 5000!) to converge generally indicates that there is very little empirical information for the specified model. So, it likely means that the model that you have defined is not a good fit to the data. My guess is that the second f2 factor is not well defined. How does the model work when only the single factor is used? And how well does it fit (e.g., via functions like M2() )? 

Phil

2016年10月12日水曜日 13時39分03秒 UTC+9 Phil Chalmers:
Hi Yutaro,

The fact that it took more than 500 EM cycles (and in your case, 5000!) to converge generally indicates that there is very little empirical information for the specified model. So, it likely means that the model that you have defined is not a good fit to the data. My guess is that the second f2 factor is not well defined. How does the model work when only the single factor is used? And how well does it fit (e.g., via functions like M2() )? 

Phil
